I am reviewing the full law text and independent analyses to ensure I have not missed a strong argument for yes.

The vote is leaning toward no. I am checking the Fulton analysis, media endorsements, and remaining law text for final confirmation. One key finding is that IRS Form 990 already includes patient care and program-related overhead in its program service expenses.

The 90% program ratio requirement is stricter than standard benchmarks. It measures against revenue rather than expenses. Surpluses and reserves count as revenue, which can lower the ratio. The findings note clinics sometimes retain 20% surpluses.

The ratio is a critical design flaw. It measures mission spending against total revenue rather than total expenses. Clinics that build reserves or pay down debt automatically fail. The penalty equals the shortfall. That penalty itself reduces operating ability.

Compliance would force clinics to waste resources. Surplus clinics must spend down reserves or reclassify expenses. Break-even clinics would need to cut administration or inflate program spending.

The Attorney General has broad discretion. They can redefine what counts as a program service and exclude current Form 990 items. This creates significant uncertainty.

The Attorney General may expand or narrow what counts as a program service. Supporters cite interpretation, IT, and nurse management. Opponents claim essential services do not qualify. The law grants this broad adjustment power without clear standards. Clinics must comply before the final definitions are known.

The penalties are severe. The full dollar shortfall is due in 30 days. A $1.6 billion aggregate shortfall would be catastrophic for cash flow.

Money held in escrow for five years only returns if the clinic hits the 90% ratio and agrees to a spending plan. The Department of Public Health can use that escrow for its own administration. If the clinic fails within five years, the funds go to workforce programs and operating capital leaves the clinics.

Waivers are available but limited. They last one year and are renewable. The standard for qualifying is high. Unexpected circumstances or going concern doubts under GAAP make them difficult to obtain.

A private right of action allows patients to sue for breach of charitable trust if a clinic falls below the 90% ratio without a waiver. This invites litigation beyond state enforcement. The title summary also indicates criminal charges for false reports or artificially inflating the spending ratio.

Enforcement fees run into the tens of millions. That further drains resources from patient care.

The measure excludes tribal and urban Indian organizations and public clinics. Only private nonprofit FQHCs and look-alikes are covered.

The union has a history of using ballot initiatives as organizing leverage. Politico reported that SEIU-UHW suggested dropping this measure if clinics allowed organizing 25,000 workers. Both major parties oppose it.

Major medical organizations oppose the measure. The voter guide lists no official supporters. The union spent relatively little on its campaign while opponents spent tens of millions. This supports the leverage theory.

The initiative findings cite excessive management spending and CEO pay up to $1.9 million. Some legitimate accountability issues may exist.

The 90% revenue rule is a blunt tool for addressing executive compensation outliers. Existing law already requires nonprofit boards to ensure CEO and CFO pay is just and reasonable. IRS intermediate sanctions, Attorney General charitable trust oversight, and HRSA FQHC requirements already provide oversight. A targeted executive compensation cap or transparency measure would be more appropriate than a broad ratio that punishes necessary reserves and administration.

FQHC revenue structures are complex. They rely on grants, 340B pharmacy programs, Medi-Cal PPS, and sliding scale pricing.

Required administrative costs such as billing, grant compliance, and quality reporting are often classified as management and general expenses. Federal grant rules frequently allow 15 percent or more of revenue for these activities. A 10 percent cap on non-program spending conflicts with established federal norms.

Facility financing also complicates the ratio. Principal payments on debt may not count as program expenses. Depreciation is an expense but does not generate cash flow for the ratio calculation.

Depreciation can be allocated to program services, yet cash from principal payments on debt may not count as program expense. This accounting mismatch is messy.

The surplus problem is the most severe flaw. A clinic that spends 85 percent of revenue on programs and retains 5 percent as surplus fails the 90 percent test. The maximum combined overhead and reserves is capped at 10 percent of revenue.

The 10 percent revenue cap is too tight for working capital. Healthcare best practice requires 30 to 90 days cash on hand, and reserves for capital, equipment, and emergencies would be constrained.

The LAO estimates state costs at low tens of millions covered by clinic fees. Uncertain costs remain if clinics spend more on Medi-Cal services or close, shifting burden to emergency rooms and counties.

Patients would likely lose care if clinics cut services or closed. Workers could benefit from workforce programs and hiring, but closures and penalties would hurt them too. The union would gain politically.

Most FQHC patients would be hurt by service cuts or closures. Well-run clinics with normal nonprofit costs would suffer. State and local budgets would face fee-funded bureaucracy and potential cost shifts.

Some clinics may have genuinely excessive executive compensation while patients wait. Transparency is a valid goal. The penalty is refundable if the clinic restructures and complies, so it functions more as a forced spend-down than a permanent tax. The going-concern waiver provides a safety valve.

permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars
to the price of a new home, driving up rents and
mortgages for homeowners and renters. Similar red
tape adds billions of dollars to the cost of building

energy, schools, broadband, and wildfire mitigation

laws were in place. That outdated system now works
against the state’s environmental and public health
goals by slowing down or blocking essential projects
that would reduce air pollution, lower greenhouse gas
emissions, safeguard water supplies, protect
communities from wildfire, and preserve wildlife and
the environment.

cut bureaucratic red tape and unnecessary delays, limit
frivolous lawsuits that block essential projects while
allowing public agencies and essential project
applicants to continue sharing the burden of defending
against those suits, and speed up delivery of projects
Californians rely on every day.

Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Community Health Clinics
Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics to Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act
Spending Requirements for Federally Qualified Health Centers Initiative
Summary
Proposition 44 began as Initiative 25-0008 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0008A1%20%28%26quot%3BClinic%20Funding%20Accountability%20and%20Transparency%20Act%26quot%3B%29.pdf), filed by Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming in July 2025. After receiving its official title and summary, the measure was cleared for signature gathering in October 2025. On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot. It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services. No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services. The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall. The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years. If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 44 would cost the state in the low tens of millions of dollars each year to enforce the new requirements, including reviewing clinic financial reports and investigating possible violations. These costs would be paid for through fees charged to the clinics as directed by the proposition.
The measure could also affect state and local government spending in other ways, but the costs are uncertain. For example, affected clinics might increase spending on direct patient care to meet the 90% requirement. Because some of those patients are covered by Medi-Cal, this could increase state health care costs. Alternatively, clinics that are unable to meet the requirement could close instead. This could also result in additional costs for state or local governments. The overall fiscal effect is uncertain and would depend largely on how the new spending rules are implemented and how clinics respond to them.
What your vote means
YES: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would be required to use at least 90 percent of their annual revenue to provide health care services.
NO: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would not be subject to the proposed 90 percent spending requirement.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that clinics regularly receive billions of dollars of taxpayer public funds but often spend it in areas not related to patient care. Proposition 44 would ensure more of the public funding received by nonprofit community health clinics goes toward patient care rather than administrative costs and executive compensation. They say the 90% spending requirement would direct more money toward health services while increasing transparency and accountability. Supporters also note that unrecovered penalties would be used to recruit, train, and retain health care workers.
Opponents argue that Proposition 44 is poorly drafted and institutes spending restrictions that could force community health clinics to cut services or close, reducing access to care. They contend that the measure could restrict spending on essential staff, equipment, technology, and other services needed to operate clinics. Opponents also argue that the measure is unnecessary because community health clinics are already subject to state and federal regulations, audits, and oversight.

I have a solid basis for voting no.

I reviewed the LAO report and text of the proposition. It mandates 90% program spending, but defines the ratio as program expenses divided by total revenue, allowing surpluses to count against it. The Attorney General can also redefine the metric. Private patients may sue clinics for violations.

Criminal penalties apply to misreporting. Waivers are restricted to exceptional circumstances or going-concerns. The amendment process is difficult.

Research by Indiana University suggests 89% of California clinics would fail the 90% ratio, with first-year fines reaching $1.6 billion. Most clinics currently in the red would be affected. The standard effectively prevents building reserves.

The Berkeley Research Group notes that a 90% ratio would block reserves for capital improvements, equipment, and emergencies.

Opposition spans both parties and major health groups. Supporters are essentially limited to one union, with no other submitted. The union previously lost similar dialysis measures and reportedly considered dropping this one for organizing access. Local newspapers have all endorsed a no vote. PPIC polling shows only 34 percent support.

The policy case against the proposition is independent of any political motive. The 90% ratio punishes financial prudence by penalizing reserves and surpluses. The threshold far exceeds actual practice, and almost no US health center meets it. Penalties equal the shortfall and must be paid within 30 days, creating a liquidity crisis. Required administrative work cannot realistically fit into 10% of revenue alongside reserves. The measure risks reducing access for the exact populations clinics serve.
